keyTakeaways: The apple-peel love charm is in print by 1714 (John Gay); its Halloween rules appear in Kelley's 1919 book.
The owl as a death omen dates to Pliny around AD 77, long before any Halloween link; Macbeth's witch cats are grey and streaked, not black.
A 1985 review of news stories from 1958 to 1983 found stranger-poisoned candy greatly exaggerated; pedestrian deaths run 43% higher on Halloween evenings.
Studies of 67,045 crimes and 17,966 psychiatric cases found no Halloween crime spike and no full-moon effect.
On SubhSandesh, 38.5% of creators password-protect their page and 48.3% of views come from phones.

faqs.question: What are the most common Halloween superstitions?
faqs.answer: The best documented are love charms (an apple peel that forms an initial, a mirror at midnight, nuts on a fire) and omens (an owl's shriek, a witch's cat, bats). Others hold that a baby born on Halloween sees spirits, a belief Walter Scott put in a novel in 1820.

faqs.question: Is it bad luck to see a black cat on Halloween?
faqs.answer: Only by modern convention. In Macbeth, written about 1606, the witches' cats are grey and streaked, and black cats join owls and bats as standard Halloween witch companions in print by 1919.

faqs.question: Should I check my child's Halloween candy for razor blades?
faqs.answer: You can, but the stranger-sadist story is largely legend. Sociologists who reviewed news reports from 1958 to 1983 found the threat greatly exaggerated; cars are the bigger risk, with pedestrian deaths 43% higher on Halloween evenings in US data.

faqs.question: What does it mean if you see a spider on Halloween?
faqs.answer: Popular lists say it is a dead loved one watching you, but we found no old source for that. It does not appear in Hone's 1825–26 notes, Lady Wilde's 1887 Irish collection or Kelley's 1919 Halloween book.

faqs.question: Why are owls linked to death and Halloween?
faqs.answer: The omen is far older than Halloween. Pliny the Elder called the horned owl a funereal bird and a direful omen around AD 77, and Macbeth calls its shriek the fatal bellman; witch imagery later carried it into October décor.

faqs.question: What happens if you look in a mirror at midnight on Halloween?
faqs.answer: By tradition, a future husband or wife appears behind you. A 1919 version adds eating an apple in nine slices by moonlight, while Lady Wilde's 1887 Irish account tells the charm as a deadly warning instead.

faqs.question: Are people born on Halloween supposed to have second sight?
faqs.answer: That was a Scottish Border belief recorded in Walter Scott's The Monastery in 1820. It is folklore; no evidence links a birth date to any unusual perception.

faqs.question: Is there more crime against children on Halloween?
faqs.answer: Not according to US national crime records from 1997 to 2005. A 2009 study of 67,045 non-family sex crimes against children aged 12 and under found no rise on or just before Halloween.

faqs.question: Does a full moon make people behave strangely?
faqs.answer: Hospital data says no. A 2019 Swiss study of 17,966 psychiatric inpatient cases found no link between moon phase and admissions, discharges or length of stay.

faqs.question: Do lucky charms actually work?
faqs.answer: Not on performance in controlled tests. Two high-powered 2014 replications found people told their golf ball was lucky performed almost identically to everyone else.

faqs.question: What day of the week is Halloween in 2026 and 2027?
faqs.answer: Halloween is always 31 October. It falls on a Saturday in 2026 and a Sunday in 2027.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Halloween Superstitions and Myths, Traced to Their Oldest Records

Halloween superstitions are beliefs tied to 31 October: that an apple peel, a mirror or a nut in the fire can reveal a future sweetheart, that an owl's shriek foretells a death, and that a child born on Halloween sees spirits. The old ones have a paper trail going back centuries. The modern Halloween myths repeated every October, such as poisoned candy from strangers and full-moon madness, mostly fail when checked against research.

The love charms were private rituals for one person, and that instinct survives online. On SubhSandesh, 38.5% of creators lock their page with a password, and phones account for 48.3% of views. Below: six old superstitions with their earliest sources, then four modern myths tested against studies.

## What separates a Halloween superstition from a Halloween myth?

A Halloween superstition is a belief that a sign or action on 31 October can reveal or change what happens next, like a charm to see a future spouse. A Halloween myth, here, is a modern claim stated as fact, such as razor blades in apples, that data can test.

Nobody treated the old charms as evidence. William Hone's Every-Day Book (issued 1825–26) calls them games of "young people", and records the night's other name, "nutcrack night", from the nuts flung into the fire.

## 6 old Halloween superstitions and the earliest source for each

Each card gives the belief, the oldest record we opened, what it says and a verdict. A date means "written down by", not "invented in".

### 1. The apple peel that spells a name

- **Belief:** throw an unbroken apple peel over your shoulder and it lands as your sweetheart's initial.
- **Earliest record:** John Gay's poem The Shepherd's Week (1714), where the paring forms "A perfect 'L'".
- **What it says:** Gay's spell has no date attached. Ruth Kelley's 1919 [Halloween party handbook](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/20644) adds the rules: swing it three times round your head and drop it behind the left shoulder.
- **Verdict:** a 300-year-old game; the Halloween timing came later.

### 2. The moonlit mirror

- **Belief:** sit at a mirror at midnight and the face of a future husband or wife shows behind you.
- **Earliest record:** Kelley (1919) prints a moonlit version: eat an apple in nine slices from a knife point, and the lover appears "asking for the last piece of apple".
- **What it says:** Lady Wilde's Ancient Legends of Ireland (1887) tells it as a warning. A servant who "played a trick" before the looking-glass was found dead the next night beside the shattered glass.
- **Verdict:** the oldest Irish account we read treats the mirror as dangerous, not romantic.

### 3. Three nuts on the grate

- **Belief:** name nuts after suitors, and the fire shows which one is faithful.
- **Earliest record:** Hone (1825–26) on Ireland: a nut on the grate that "cracks or jumps" marks an unfaithful lover; one that blazes shows he "has a regard" for her.
- **What it says:** Hone credits the antiquary John Brand, so this is compiled, not observed.
- **Verdict:** a loyalty test for an existing suitor, not a charm to find a new one.

### 4. The owl's shriek

- **Belief:** an owl near a house foretells a death.
- **Earliest record:** Pliny the Elder's Natural History (about AD 77) calls the horned owl "especially funereal" and a "direful omen" inside a city.
- **What it says:** Pliny adds that it is "not portentous of evil" on a private house. Shakespeare's Macbeth (about 1606) calls it "the fatal bellman" on a murder night.
- **Verdict:** an omen for nearly 1,950 years, with no Halloween link in either text.

### 5. Bats and the witch's cat

- **Belief:** black cats and bats serve witches, so meeting one on Halloween is bad luck.
- **Earliest record:** Macbeth's cauldron takes "Wool of bat", but the witches' cats are Graymalkin, a grey cat, and a "brinded", or streaked, one. Neither is black.
- **What it says:** Kelley (1919) has witches "attended by black cats, owls, bats, and toads", and claims the animals were once sacred to Freya without citing anything.
- **Verdict:** the cat, bat and owl trio was party décor by 1919; the Freya origin is unsupported.

### 6. Born on Halloween, born with second sight

- **Belief:** a baby born on Halloween can see spirits.
- **Earliest record:** Walter Scott's novel The Monastery (1820): "they that are born on Hallowe'en whiles see mair than ither folk".
- **What it says:** fiction, voiced as ordinary Border belief about the girl Mary Avenel.
- **Verdict:** a documented folk belief, not a documented ability.

One popular claim fails even the paper test: that a spider seen on Halloween is a dead relative watching over you. It is absent from Hone, Wilde and Kelley, whose only spiders sleep in a poem.

## 4 modern Halloween myths checked against research

The modern myths changed real behaviour, from X-raying sweets to keeping people off streets. That earns them a harder test.

### 1. Strangers poison candy or hide razor blades in apples

Sociologists Joel Best and Gerald Horiuchi reviewed news stories of "Halloween sadism" from 1958 to 1983 for Social Problems in June 1985. Their [paper on the razor blade in the apple](https://doi.org/10.1525/sp.1985.32.5.03a00070) finds the threat "greatly exaggerated", an urban legend from the early 1970s (abstract read; full text paywalled).

The documented danger is traffic. A [2019 research letter in JAMA Pediatrics](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC6583441) set 42 years of Halloween evenings against the evenings a week either side: 608 pedestrian deaths against 851 across twice as many nights. That is a 43% rise in risk, and a tenfold rise for walkers between 4 and 8 years old.

### 2. Shelters stop black-cat adoptions in October

True of the past, weak today. [Kentucky public-shelter records analysed by Carini and colleagues (2020)](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC7597961) note that HSUS concedes the old October practice of withholding black cats, yet the authors saw "a paucity of empirical evidence" of worse treatment at Halloween.

Colour mattered all year instead: black cats had a 74.6% euthanasia rate against 63.0% for white cats. And 1,219 all-black cats did no better in October than in other months, so ask your local shelter rather than assume.

### 3. Crimes against children spike on Halloween

US states, towns and parole boards have barred registered sex offenders from Halloween activities. Mark Chaffin and three co-authors tested the premise in 2009 with national crime reports from 1997 to 2005: 67,045 non-family sex crimes against children aged 12 and under.

They found no rise on or just before Halloween. The authors questioned spending police time on "a problem that does not appear to exist".

### 4. The full moon makes the night wilder

Lunar madness is an old belief that hospital records do not support. A [Swiss Medical Weekly study of 17,966 psychiatric inpatient cases (2019)](https://smw.ch/index.php/smw/article/view/2616) tested 20 moon-phase categories and found no link with admissions, discharges or length of stay.

## Halloween superstitions and myths compared

This table groups the claims above with the oldest record we read and the evidence. We have no Halloween usage figures of our own, so it carries no first-party column.

| Claim | Oldest record read | What the evidence shows | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Peel, mirror or nuts reveal a sweetheart | 1714 (Gay), 1825–26 (Hone), 1887 (Wilde) | Games; nothing to measure | Folklore, harmless |
| Owl, bat or cat as an omen | About AD 77 (Pliny), about 1606 (Macbeth) | Omens predate any Halloween link | Folklore |
| Poisoned treats from strangers | News stories from 1958 | 25 years of press reports: exaggerated | Myth |
| Black cats at risk in October | Past shelter practice (HSUS) | 1,219 black cats: no October change | Mostly myth |
| Full moon or crime spike | Ancient "lunacy"; crime data 1997–2005 | 17,966 cases, 67,045 crimes: no effect | Myth |

The old superstitions were fun with no claim to proof. The modern myths claimed proof and lack it.

## Why people keep Halloween superstitions anyway

Lucky charms do not change outcomes in controlled tests. In two high-powered replications published in Social Psychology in 2014, [players told their golf ball was lucky](https://doi.org/10.1027/1864-9335/a000190) performed almost identically to players given an ordinary ball. Only the abstract was available to us.

The old charms survive because they were social. Hone quotes Robert Burns, who called fortune-telling on this night "the passion of prying into futurity" and found it in "all ages and nations".

## Sending one Halloween charm to one person

Nearly every charm above aimed at one face, a single future sweetheart. A greeting page does that job openly for one person, and nine in ten started pages on SubhSandesh (90.9%) end up published.

The [haunted-house Halloween card with a pumpkin to carve](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween) is a roughly five-minute build. The recipient knocks, carves the word you chose until the candle lights, finds your letter in a dark attic and mixes a potion from three to five of your memories. It holds six photos at most and closes on the boo question.

The [cinematic premium Halloween page that plays your recorded voice](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween-premium) needs closer to ten minutes. You get a 60-second voice note, room for 12 photos, a lock until a time you set, and one written reply sent to your inbox.

If the charm you really want is the old one, learning whether someone will go out with you, ask outright. The [invitation page with a yes-or-no answer](https://subhsandesh.in/date-invitation) converts a yes into a countdown to the day.

## When folklore, or our page, is the wrong call

Folklore is not safety advice. On the 2019 road data, reflective clothing and a crossing plan protect trick-or-treaters more than checking every wrapper.

- **Sincere belief:** many Pagans keep Samhain as a sacred festival, so a joke card about omens can land badly.
- **A party:** both Halloween pages greet one person, in English only, and cannot invite a group.
- **Wide reach:** each page here draws 11.1 views on average.

Best & Horiuchi, 'The Razor Blade in the Apple: The Social Construction of Urban Legends', Social Problems 32(5):488-499, June 1985 (Crossref: publisher now Oxford University Press; DOI prefix 10.1525 = University of California Press, the 1985 publisher for SSSP). Carini, Sinski & Weber, 'Coat Color and Cat Outcomes in an Urban U.S. Shelter', Animals 10(10):1720 (MDPI, CC BY), full text read: 7,983 cats, Kentucky public shelter 2010-2011; black cats euthanasia 74.6% vs white 63.0%; 1,219 entirely black cats' October adoption/transfer comparable to or lower than other months; HSUS acknowledges shelters once pulled black cats from adoption around Halloween; 'a paucity of empirical evidence' black cats fare worse at Halloween.

Gupta, Nolan, Bux & Schneeberger, 'Is it the moon? Effects of the lunar cycle on psychiatric admissions, discharges and length of stay', Swiss Medical Weekly 149:w20070 (open access): 17,966 inpatient cases, Canton Grisons; 20 moon-phase categories; no connection with admission or discharge rates or length of stay.

Calin-Jageman & Caldwell, 'Replication of the Superstition and Performance Study by Damisch, Stoberock, and Mussweiler (2010)', Social Psychology 45(3):239-245 (Hogrefe, open access CC BY-NC-ND), abstract only (publisher page 403): two high-powered replications; participants told they had a lucky golf ball performed almost identically to controls on a 10-shot task; meta-analysis shows heterogeneity.

structuralLimitations: No Halloween usage data exists in facts.md; the four first-party figures are platform-wide and are not presented as Halloween data.

Prompt said b5 found 'shelters don't ban black cats'. Re-verified in Carini 2020 full text: the paper does not survey shelter policy; it reports that HSUS acknowledges shelters once pulled black cats around Halloween (and cites a 2016 Smithsonian piece, 403 to us, implying some still did). Body says 'true of the past, weak today' and advises asking the local shelter.

Best & Horiuchi 1985: Crossref lists the current publisher as Oxford University Press; the DOI prefix 10.1525 is University of California Press, which published Social Problems for SSSP in 1985. No open copy found (OpenAlex is_oa false); OUP page 403. Only the abstract was read, and the body says so; incident counts from the full paper are NOT used.

Chaffin, Levenson, Letourneau & Stern 2009 (Sexual Abuse 21(3)) is SAGE, a banned publisher in this batch; its abstract (via OpenAlex) is described in the body and the Sources list but deliberately NOT linked and NOT in batchMeta.sources/citation.
